Definitions
Fairness
ensures that there is an absence of any discrimination or favoritism
toward an individual or a group
based on any inherent or acquired characteristics that are irrelevant
in the context of decision making
Accountability
refers to the need to explain and justify the actions and decisions
made by the system to different users with whom the system
interacts
Privacy
sensitive data that is either shared by an individual or collected by an
AI system
protected from any unjustifiable or illegal gathering and use of data

Types of Bias
Data Bias : Crucial to make the data fair and diverse
If the data on which the system is trained is biased
Data does not represent a clear picture of reality
If the training data has representation or societal bias
Representation bias
data does not represent all segments of society equally
Societal bias
data correctly represents the society that is already biased
If the population demographics of the training dataset are entirely
different from the target population on which the system is being
implemented

Model bias:
Imperative to carefully select objective functions and features
If the algorithm itself introduces it
Example :
System designed to predict the need for treatment based on the level
of patient illness
was observed to be favorably biased toward healthier white patients
than sick black patients

benefits

Individual Fairness
Fairness in classification, where individuals are classified
Example Scenario : University
Prevent discrimination against individuals based on their membership
in some group
Scenario : Credit Card Company
Tracks to learn detailed demographic information about each visitor
to the site
Approximate income, where she shops, other expenditures, etc.
Can lead to minority groups into less advantageous credit
Any two individuals who are similar with respect to a particular task
should be classified similarly
Assume a distance metric that defines the similarity between the
individuals

Counterfactual Fairness
A decision is fair towards an individual if it is the same
the actual world
a counterfactual world where the individual belonged to a different
demographic group
An algorithm is fair so long as any protected attributes A are not
explicitly used in the decision-making process.
A predictor Y satisfies demographic parity if P (Y ) given (A = 0) is
same as P (Y ) given (A = 1)

A car insurance company wishes to price insurance for car owners by
predicting their accident rate Y

Counterfactual Fairness
Individuals belonging to a certain race A are more likely to drive red
cars
these individuals are no more likely to be aggressive
or, to get in accidents than any one else
Summary of Insights
using the red car feature X to predict accident rate Y would seem to
be an unfair prediction
Reasoning it may charge individuals of a certain race more than
others,
even though no race is more likely to have an accident
Counterfactual fairness agrees with this notion: changing A while
holding U fixed will also change X and, consequently, Y

a registry of residents containing their neighborhood X and race A,

High Crime Regions
Locations X with more police resources have larger numbers of
arrests Y
higher observed arrest rates in some neighborhoods are due to
greater policing there,
not because people of different races are any more or less likely to
break the law
Also, Y = 0 does not mean someone has never committed a crime,
but, rather that they have not been caught.

Representation Bias
Representation bias arises from how we sample from a population
during data collection process
Selected samples lack the required diversity of the population
Gender dataset for gender related events
Consideration of race
Language consideration
Non-representative samples lack the diversity of the population
with missing subgroups and other anomalies
Sampling Bias
Similar to representation bias
Arises due to non random sampling of subgroups
Result the trends estimated for one population may not generalize to
data collected from a new population

Aggregation Bias
Aggregation bias arises when false conclusions are drawn about
individuals from observing the entire population
Simpson’s Paradox
when an association observed in aggregated data disappears or
reverses
when the same data is disaggregated into its underlying subgroups
Gender Bias lawsuit in university admissions against UCBerkeley
it seemed there was bias toward women
a smaller fraction of whom were being admitted to graduate
programs compared male counterparts
However,when admissions data was separated and analyzed over the
departments
women applicants had equality and in some cases even a small
advantage
paradox happened as women tended to apply to departments with
lower admission rates for both genders
